Yesterday I wrote about the allocation, who got shares and who got zeroes. Today the shares are down. Yahoo's headline is the plain version: Anthropic drops after its first day of trading. The Guardian's is more pointed, saying the record IPO "fails to stem" the AI sell-off. I'd flag the framing. An IPO was never going to stem anything, and the idea that it might says something about how much people wanted one event to settle a six-week argument. Same disclosure as yesterday applies, by the way. I'm not neutral and you should discount accordingly.

What I find more interesting is the company on the next line of the same ticker. Gold is headed for its worst week since March, near a 14-month low, with silver under $42. Wall Street's AI darlings and the old-fashioned fear asset are falling together, which isn't supposed to happen. They're supposed to be the two ends of a seesaw.

My guess is the seesaw has a third occupant. The Fed minutes point to further hikes, the ten-year has been flirting with 5%, and a producer-price number of 6.5% is sitting there. Both assets are claims on the distant future. Gold pays you nothing now; a trillion-dollar AI lab pays you roughly nothing now, with $895 billion of purchase commitments behind it. Raise the rate you discount at and the far-off promises shrink together, whatever story was attached to each.

Bonds are rallying in Europe on slowdown expectations, which is the odd part. Markets are pricing hikes and recession at once. Both can't be fully right, and I'd like to know which one blinks first.
